title: Currently developing a RogueLite with Claude Code
author: BBmanse
selftext:
Its been always a dream of mine to develop my own game, but ive recivied some discouraging comments from close friends which ive showed my advances related to the use of AI in my project. Also read about it in a few places where seems to be that all the hard work ive been putting into this means nothing cause claude as my coder and nano banana for sprites.

Im really enjoying this experience and im building the game i would like to play. I do believe this is a huge door for new indie developers and it will change things in a positive ways.

Any advices for a first time developer?

comments.author: Whole_Toe4911
comments.body: many ai games here are shitty because desinging a good game is still hard even with AI. plus its easy to generate a huge game without paying attention to any details.

comments.author: PotentialBet5419
comments.body: Don't over scope play test everything organize your agents.  Give them roles and have them cross check each othera work make sure to take screenshots and record the bugs that pop up give direct  intentional orders and that gets you a long way.

replies.author: BBmanse
replies.body: Thats one thing i wish i would done better, i think i went a bit too ambitious at first now i kinda want to shrink up

replies.author: PotentialBet5419
replies.body: Scale down where you can. Don't loose the feel of your game you can cut and splice mechanics id draw up a plan dissect where you can cut and I'd focus on feel and cohesive gameplay best of luck !

comments.author: GlobalCurry
comments.body: I mostly use AI to build prototypes, systems, and tooling, but handcraft levels, balancing, and such unless it's a proc gen game. Making sure the experience is good is what matters, and where "ai slop" and "asset flip" games fail.

comments.author: Blake9712
comments.body: Just keep at it. Don’t get discouraged by shallow one shots you see posted and don’t expect to be done in a day or even a month. A deep rogue lite may take years of part time or a year of full time even if you’re using ai. Or it may take less. But don’t rush it and make the best game that you can that you’d enjoy. Make sure you understand what is fun about your game and what the hook is.

comments.author: gamerqc
comments.body: Don't mind the haters. It's mostly virtue signaling at this point. I'm building a prototype too and just paid for MAX (x5) because I'm enjoying it a lot and want to go deeper. Keep at it and do listen to feedback, but people who equate AI = bad are very shortsighted because most of the industry is shifting that way.

comments.author: TryCool2339
comments.body:
1. The discouraging comments are just a fact of life.  Take what's useful from them, leave the bias / gatekeeping / judgement behind, and move forward.  Many people are irrationally tribal about their AI hate (it's more of a social belonging-driven lifestyle choice than an actual evidence-backed belief).  And remember, not everyone has earned an opinion about everything!  Ask your friends to focus on the substance of the game, not the methods you used to produce it.  You're not obligated to share your methods!

2. Do it for yourself.  You've always wanted to do this, so why do the opinions of others matter?  Do it for your own learning and enjoyment, journal the process so you can remember what it was like to be down in the trenches with your AI of choice several months from now.

3. Test test test!  Nothing gives away an amateur job faster than failing on the basics.  Make sure all the simple stuff works perfectly and feels good to interact with.  Detailed mechanics are background and can be tuned through playtesting and player feedback over time.

4. Don't just accept the first thing the AI produces for you; iterate on every feature and asset and let your own taste develop and influence the project.  The only way your effort doesn't matter, is if you let the AI make most of the creative decisions via RNG / the average of its training data.  "Looks good to me" will get you to Slop Town real fast.  If you give your AI a pass on something for the sake of making progress, be sure to note it as temporary and leave a TODO to come back to it later to adjust/improve/put your own spin on it.  Worst thing you can do is have the AI make the decision by default, then come back later wondering if it was your idea or not.  Document your work!

Now go get 'em!

comments.author: John_Champaign
comments.body:
I think creating a RogueLite with Claude Code is a great project.  Can't comment on your friends, but I'd guess they're either just Debbie Downers (are they always making discouraging comments?) or you made something too big.  

I'd pull back and work on something similar to a RogueLite you've enjoyed playing.  Either do a mod for it or a clean room reverse engineering of it.  Make a tight, focused modication - make a single game play change, add some new elements, or make a cosmetic only change to it.  

Evaluate, get feedback from people worth listening to, then iterate (work on a larger change or your own small project eventually).
